items.prompt: An invented position–time line passes through (0 s, 2 cm) and (5 s, 22 cm). Calculate its gradient and give its unit.
items.canonical_answer: The vertical change is 20 cm and the horizontal change is 5 s. Gradient = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cm/s.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution working: use vertical change divided by horizontal change, 1 mark.
Answer: 4 cm/s with the axis-ratio unit, 1 mark.

items.prompt: A straight position–time line begins at 2 cm when time is zero. Explain whether position is directly proportional to this elapsed time.
items.canonical_answer: It is not directly proportional to this elapsed time because its line misses the origin; the 2 cm intercept is evidence.
marking_guidance: Conclusion: no direct proportionality to the stated time, 1 mark.
Evidence: use the nonzero position at zero time, 1 mark.

items.prompt: A set of trolley positions is recorded at one-second intervals. Describe one comparison that could support a constant-speed conclusion.
items.canonical_answer: Compare successive changes in position across the equal time intervals; approximately equal changes support a constant rate.
marking_guidance: One method step: compare position changes during equal time intervals, 1 mark.

items.prompt:
The following readings are invented for practice.

| Time / s | Position / cm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 2 |
| 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 10 |
| 3 | 14 |
| 4 | 18 |
| 5 | 22 |

(a) Draw a graph of position against time with a fitted line. [5]
(b) Calculate the gradient, showing its construction on your graph. [3]
(c) Explain whether position is directly proportional to elapsed time, using the data or graph. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Time / s is horizontal and position / cm vertical. Use uniform scales occupying at least half the grid, plot all six points and fit the line through the trend. The line crosses the position axis at 2 cm.
(b) A triangle between (0 s, 2 cm) and (5 s, 22 cm) gives a rise of 20 cm and a run of 5 s; 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cm/s.
(c) It is not direct proportionality to the stated elapsed time: the line has a nonzero position intercept. Equal changes in equal time instead support a constant rate of position change.
marking_guidance: Graph: axes with quantity/unit (1), suitable scales (1), all six points (2), fitted line (1).
Gradient: visible large construction (1), slope calculation (1), axis-ratio unit (1).
Conclusion: correct relationship judgement (1), supporting intercept evidence (1).

items.prompt: Plan a test of how pulling force changes a spring’s increase in length. Include the arrangement, measurements, variables, a table and a way to reach a conclusion. Use calibrated loads and safe forces. [8]
items.canonical_answer: For a spring investigation, secure the spring vertically and record its unloaded length against a nearby ruler. Add a calibrated force and measure the new length after the spring settles. Subtract the unloaded length to obtain extension, then repeat at several safe forces. Use the same spring, the same reference points and the same reading method. Keep falling loads away from feet and avoid overloading the spring. Record force in newtons, unloaded and loaded length in millimetres, and calculated extension in millimetres. Plot extension vertically against force horizontally. Describe the trend from the plotted data; if a fitted straight line is suitable, its gradient has units of millimetres per newton. Do not call that gradient a spring constant: the spring constant uses force per extension.
marking_guidance: Method: secure the spring (1), measure unloaded length (1), apply a known force (1), measure the new length using a ruler (1), repeat with several forces (1).
Table: clear headings and units for force and the lengths needed to obtain extension (1).
Graph: extension against force with labelled axes (1).
Conclusion: use the measured trend or the fitted graph to answer the aim (1).
Controls and safety: keep the spring and reading method unchanged and avoid overload or falling loads; these support the stated method rather than creating additional marks.
